newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian economy is not all that it seems.
newsitem.headline: Russian economy is not all that it seems.

text.p: All is not what it seems in the Russian economy, where poor output figures hide a booming black economy and firms play down success for fear of paying tax.

Ministers lobby in public for the 1997 budget draft but say privately the plans are unrealistic. Companies earning billions of dollars are threatened with bankruptcy and the government is crying out for cash.

"We all know that the Russian economy is not booming by any stretch of the imagination but I am not sure that it is in the state of decline that the official statistics suggest," said one Western economist.
The official figures -- dubbed a virtual economy by some analysts -- show that tight monetary policies of the last two years have dragged inflation down and ended the rouble's roller-coaster ride.

But the International Monetary Fund, worried about lower than expected tax collection, has postponed paying tranches of a $10 billion three-year loan and the government has threatened to declare tax debtors bankrupt to force them to pay.
Companies under threat of bankruptcy have included several major firms in the crucial energy sector and car giant Avtovaz, Russia's fifth biggest employer with 114,000 workers.

Analysts say Russian statistics have improved since experts started using Western methods to assess growth, inflation and other indicators, but even Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin admits he does not know the size of the untaxed shadow economy.
"The specialists cannot say exactly how much of the economy is in the grey zone," Interfax news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying. "The spread is from 20 to 50 percent."
Official figures, reassessed after World Bank complaints that statisticians were ignoring the grey economy, say it accounts for 22 percent of gross domestic product.
"The statistics are better than they used to be, but they have still got problems," said Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital.

"They do not pick up the grey economy as much as they should and even the State Statistics Committee gets confused because there are different figures for industrial output for large and medium sized enterprises and for the economy as a whole."

Analysts said new problems would emerge next year unless the government and parliament reach a deal on the 1997 budget, due to be discussed next week. Communists and liberals have criticised the plan.

"The budget is absolutely unacceptable to us," Grigory Yavlinsky, leader of the liberal Yabloko political movement said on Thursday. "Economic policy is erroneous and incomplete...we are falling ever deeper into an economic crisis."
The view is backed, at least in part, by Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin who said urgent action was needed to propel Russia towards growth.

"If the existing trends in the economy are continued without energetic efforts to...create real conditions for growth, the situation will in all probability continue to get worse," Yasin wrote in a letter to Chernomyrdin.
"Growth is...totally imperative for survival and for economic and political stability."
Yasin, outlining industrial policy for 1997, said Russia would give subsidies and investment funds to some key industries but would tell others to stand on their own feet.

Analysts said Yasin's industrial policy could increase pressure on ministers to follow an inflationary course, but said there were few signs that the government was ready to throw away the gains brought by two years of high interest rates.

Year-on-year inflation -- 27.2 percent in October -- is at its lowest level since Russian economic reforms began. But industrial output, which has halved over the same period, fell four percent in the year to October.
Ministers have denied they will print money to help industry recover and say policy will target the need for low inflation.
Officials plan to hold the rouble within a so-called sloping corridor for the whole of next year, allowing the rouble a steady, but gentle daily decline.
"The decision...means the question of mass issue of money...is evidently ruled out as a practical policy," Finance Minister Alexander Livshits said when he announced the plans.
